title: What it is not
hook: the Abhidhamma is one way of looking, not a test anyone must pass

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mirror carried through a whole ordinary day, three factors once an hour. Your line: a day of noticing. Which hour surprised you? Day one thousand ninety-five.

Fifty-two mental factors. Twenty-eight kinds of matter. Twenty-four conditions. After all these lists, a fair question rises up: does a person have to learn all this? Is there an exam at the end of the path, a long sheet of Pali with blanks to fill in? The Theravada tradition has its own answer, and it comes in a story about an old man who never opened the books. Today: what the Abhidhamma is not.
screen: `FIFTY-TWO, TWENTY-EIGHT, TWENTY-FOUR.` → `IS THERE AN EXAM?` → `AN OLD MAN WITHOUT THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, two duties. In the commentary on the Dhammapada, a man who has become a monk late in life asks the Buddha what the duties are in this teaching. There are two, the story says. One is the duty of the books: learning the texts, studying, keeping the words. The other is the duty of insight: watching body and mind until you see how they really are. Second, the old monk chooses. He says, in paraphrase: I came to this late, I'm too old for the books, teach me the second. And he's taught a meditation practice, and goes off to sit. The story goes on to tell how far he went with it. Nobody in the story tells him he chose wrong. Both duties are honored, and the Theravada tradition has kept both: monks and lay people who study the lists closely, and monks and lay people whose whole practice is the sitting. Third, the lists aren't one fixed answer. Remember the Sarvastivada's Abhidharma, the other school's list. It counts some things differently. Two careful traditions, looking at the same mind, drew two maps. That alone says something. A map is a way of looking. It isn't the ground you walk on. Fourth, what that leaves. The Abhidhamma is a gift some people love: precise, patient, endless. For others it's a mirror they pick up now and then. For some it never comes off the shelf. None of that is a pass or a fail. The test, if there is one, is the old monk's: does the looking help you see?
screen: `TWO DUTIES: BOOKS AND INSIGHT.` · `THE OLD MONK CHOOSES THE SITTING.` · `TWO SCHOOLS DREW TWO MAPS.` · then, large: `A WAY OF LOOKING, NOT A TEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: hold the lists lightly. Open one hand on your knee, palm up. Let it rest there, loose, as if a small list were lying in it, something you could close your fingers around or let slide off. Sit with the breath. If a name comes, restless, calm, doubt, let it sit on the open palm. Don't grip it. Don't throw it away. Let the breath and the open hand do the work. The bell holds the time.
What it is not. The Abhidhamma isn't an exam the path sets. It's one way of looking, honored alongside the duty of simply sitting and seeing. Today's word.
Your line: one way of looking. Today, when you catch yourself grading your own practice, open a hand, and let the grade go. Day one thousand ninety-five.

howItsDone: In Theravada communities, some monks and lay people devote years to studying the Abhidhamma, while others give their practice mainly to meditation; the tradition honors both study and insight.

trapdoor: what you thought: to practice Buddhism you have to master the Abhidhamma.
what it means: the lists are one way of looking, and the duty of sitting and seeing is honored beside them.
what a scholar hears: the commentarial pair of duties, the burden of books and the burden of insight, from the story of the elder Cakkhupala at the opening of the Dhammapada commentary.
recall: a factor that colors the knowing

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary on verse 1 (the story of the elder Cakkhupala), the two duties
Abhidhammattha Sangaha (the counts of mental factors, kinds of matter and conditions)

notes: The two duties (gantha-dhura and vipassana-dhura) are from the Cakkhupala story in the Dhammapada commentary; the script paraphrases the elder's reason (old age) and leaves out the later part of his story (his blindness and awakening). Confirm.
Counts in the hook (52 factors, 28 kinds of matter, 24 conditions) are those named on days 1072, 1082 and 1087 from the Abhidhammattha Sangaha and the Patthana; check they match.
'After a month of lists' refers to this block (days 1062 on); it is a description of the path, not a claim about the tradition.
'The Sarvastivada's Abhidharma counts some things differently' is stated generally (e.g. 75 dharmas in the Kosha); no number given.
